title: More blessed to give (Acts 20:17–38)
hook: Paul's farewell at Miletus; they weep and kneel on the shore

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eutychus, asleep in the window while Paul talked till dawn. Your line was even Paul went on.

A beach at Miletus, on the coast of Asia. Paul is in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, so he doesn't go up to Ephesus, where he spent about three years. Instead he sends for the elders of the Ephesian church, and they make the journey down to the shore. He tells them plainly: I don't know what will happen to me in Jerusalem, except that prison and hardship are waiting. And you will not see my face again.
screen: `A BEACH AT MILETUS.` → `THE ELDERS OF EPHESUS.` → `YOU WILL NOT SEE MY FACE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Paul's farewell sounds like a man setting his affairs in order. He reminds them how he lived among them: serving the Lord with humility and tears, holding nothing back, teaching in public and from house to house. He tells them to keep watch over the flock, like shepherds. Then he holds up his hands. I've coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing. These hands, he says, worked for my own needs and for those who were with me. Then he gives them a saying of Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "remember the word of the Lord Jesus, how he said: It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive." Here's the surprise: those words of Jesus aren't in any of the four Gospels. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John never record them. It's a saying of Jesus preserved only here, in Paul's mouth, passed along by Luke, kept by people who remembered it. And Paul isn't asking the elders for money. He's showing them his own work-worn hands and saying: this is how to lead. Give. Then the ending. Paul kneels down on the shore and prays with them all. They weep, embrace him, and kiss him, grieving most of all, the text says, because he told them they would not see his face again. And they walk him to the ship.
screen: `HUMILITY, TEARS, NOTHING HELD BACK.` · `THESE HANDS WORKED FOR MY NEEDS.` · `A SAYING FOUND IN NO GOSPEL.` · `KNEELING ON THE SHORE.` · then, large: `MORE BLESSED TO GIVE, RATHER THAN TO RECEIVE.`

segments.voice: Look at your hands, the way Paul held up his, and ask what they've given lately. Think of one thing you could give freely, without being asked, not necessarily money: time, a meal, a compliment you meant to say, help with a task, something you own that someone else needs more, and picture handing it over without waiting for thanks. If you pray, offer your hands for whatever giving the day brings.
Blessed. The word Jesus used in a saying kept only by Paul, on a beach at Miletus: it is more blessed to give than to receive. Today's word.
Your line: coveted no one's silver. Tomorrow, Jerusalem, and the steps of a barracks. Day five hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics practice almsgiving, one of the three traditional disciplines of Lent alongside prayer and fasting, and give to the poor through parish collections and works of mercy throughout the year.

original.note: Greek: blessed, the same word family as the Beatitudes. more blessed is it to give.

trapdoor: what you thought: a proverb from the Gospels.
what it means: a saying of Jesus remembered by Paul at a tearful farewell, as he holds up his own work-worn hands.
what a scholar hears: sayings of Jesus found outside the four Gospels are called agrapha, unwritten sayings. Acts 20:35 is a standard New Testament example.
recall: the assembly, Luke's word for church

chat.says: Is "it's more blessed to give than to receive" from the Gospels?
options: No: it's a saying of Jesus that Paul quotes in Acts, and no Gospel records it.
Yes, Jesus says it in the Sermon on the Mount, in Matthew's Gospel.
No, it's a line Paul wrote himself in his letter to the Romans.
chat.meaning: Paul tells the Ephesian elders to remember the words of the Lord Jesus. The saying is kept here in Acts, not in any of the four Gospels.

Miletus.meaning: a town on the coast of Asia

Ephesus.meaning: the city where Paul spent about three years

elders.meaning: the leaders of the church at Ephesus

coveted.meaning: wanted what belongs to someone else

sources.quoted: remember the word of the Lord Jesus, how he said: It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive.

notes: 'About three years' in Ephesus follows Acts 20:31; Miletus to Ephesus roughly thirty miles (about fifty km) as traveled; confirm.
'The only speech in Acts that Paul makes to Christians': a common observation; confirm.
Agrapha: confirm term and that Acts 20:35 is the standard example.
